lines: One team's deployment goes from a few hundred scheduled workflow files to several thousand, almost overnight.
Nobody expects the scheduler to get twice as slow. It gets a lot worse than that.
To see why, you first have to know what pieces are actually doing the work.
A working orchestrator needs four required parts, and only four.
A scheduler, which decides what should run now.
A dag processor, which parses the workflow files and is always its own separate process, so the scheduler never has to run code a workflow author wrote.
An a p i server, which fronts the user interface and the rest api.
And a metadata database, which holds the state of every run.
Here's the part people get wrong: the executor is not a fifth piece sitting next to these four. It is a setting on the scheduler itself, and it runs inside the scheduler's own process.
That one setting comes in three common shapes.
The local executor keeps the scheduler and every worker in one process, on one machine.
The celery executor adds a message broker and a pool of long running workers, so tasks run somewhere else entirely.
The kubernetes executor starts a brand new pod for every single task, and tears it down when the task finishes.
Here's a question before I tell you the answer.
Two scheduler processes point at the same metadata database at the same time.
Does any task ever get claimed, and scheduled, by both of them?
Think about it for a second before I reveal it.
steps.answer: No. A row lock that skips a row instead of waiting for it means a second scheduler simply moves on to the next available row, so no task is ever claimed twice.

lines: Here is that guarantee, run for real, not just described.
Two separate scheduler threads, ten real rows in one shared queue table, each thread racing the other to claim the next row.
Every single run split those ten rows cleanly between the two threads, with zero rows claimed twice.
The trick is that the lock only has to survive from the moment a row is claimed to the moment that claim is committed. It doesn't need to hold for the whole task.
Now the parsing cost itself, also measured directly, not estimated.
A real dag processor, parsing a few hundred workflow files, took well under a second.
The same processor, parsing a thousand files, took a couple of seconds.
And parsing five thousand files took around ten seconds.
Notice what stayed almost constant: the cost per file. What grew was simply the total, in direct proportion to how many files there were.
So why does that matter more than it sounds like it should?
Every single state change, for every task, is a write the metadata database has to absorb.
That database is very often the thing that actually strains first, long before the scheduler process's own processor usage looks like a problem.
A dashboard that shows a healthy, idle looking scheduler can still be sitting on top of a database that is quietly falling behind.
One more fact worth carrying forward: airflow two is on a documented path to end of life in April of twenty twenty six, well before airflow three's own current line even has an end date set.
So: four required parts, with the executor living inside the scheduler, not beside it.
Three executor shapes, trading one process for more isolation and more moving parts.
One coordination trick, a lock that skips instead of waiting, measured with zero double claims.
And one real cost curve: parsing time that grows with every file, not a fixed cost paid once.
One more scenario before we move on.
After a migration, a deployment's workflow file count jumps overnight. Not one individual workflow actually changed.
What's the first thing worth profiling?
Give it a second.
steps.answer: Parsing cost and metadata-database writes, not the scheduler process's own CPU — exactly what the last two measurements already showed, since both of those scale directly with file count.
